content.text:
Thoughts only, nothing edited. I measured both questions first so the placement argument rests on counts rather than impression.

## Hyphenation: mostly a compliance gap, with one open half

Across `AGENTS.md`, `custom.md`, and `agent-data/*`:

- `work-repo` 12 vs `work repo` 6, and `agent-repo` 14 vs `agent repo` 7.
- Every other coined compound is already single-spelled: `agent-files` 39/0, `version-of-record` 32/0, `dual-repo` 6/0, `fast-forward` 9/0, `as-built` 22/0.
- The 9 `closeout` hits are all `<closeout>`, the trapezoid recipe's revset placeholder. That is a code token, not prose, and a sweep must leave it alone.

So the drift is 13 sites in two files, 10 in `jj.md` and 3 in `AGENTS.md`, and Terminology already decided the spelling ("written hyphenated"). That half is a rung, not a cycle.

The open half is where the rule lives. Terminology is a glossary, and a glossary is read for meaning, not for spelling, so the rule is invisible to whoever is actually writing prose. The prose rules live in `prose.md`.

**Where I would put it:** a bullet under Todo #1. That entry already widens hard rule 8 from "Typeable punctuation" to "Prose style" and gathers the wall-of-prose rule under it. "A coined term has one spelling" is the third member of that same set, so one cycle states it in `prose.md`, hard rule 8 names it, and the same cycle fixes the 13 sites. Splitting it out means a second cycle re-opening the same rule and the same section days later.

**Worth proposing narrowly.** Say that a term the family coins has one spelling, fixed in Terminology, and that prose never varies it. That is greppable and finishable. A general "hyphenate compound modifiers" English rule is neither, and it invites a sweep with no end condition.

## Restart after a close-out: a new rule, no existing home

Nothing in the pinned set says anything about session lifetime, so this is not a compliance gap like the first one.

- It is family-universal. Every member's agent accumulates context and every member has close-outs, so it is a pinned-file edit, not `custom.md`.
- The agent cannot execute it, which decides what the rule can say: at the end of the close-out the agent states that the session should be restarted before the next opening, and stops. That half is checkable, and the restart itself stays yours.
- Its moment is specific, so I would put it in `AGENTS.md`'s Close-out list rather than Working practices. Backfill is already the "this happens at the next opening" step, and the restart sits exactly between the two. Working practices is a grab-bag and would bury it.
- It owes a `rationale.md` entry under the mirrored heading. The why is the substance here, and it is worth being careful about its status: that a long context degrades recall is a claim about model behavior we have not measured in this repo, so as written by the agent it takes the "We think" marker. Stated as your own repeated observation it is an observation, and can say so.

**Where I would put it:** its own `## Todo` entry alongside #1 and #2, not a bullet on either. Those two are about how rules are written and where they live, and this one adds a step to the cycle protocol, a different surface.

## On the span: 1-7 is not the series

Worth settling before you rank anything. Of Todo 1-7, only #1 and #2 are agent-files work. #3, #4, and #5 are the vc-config and global-config code cycles, #6 is validate-repo-data, #7 is trapezoid-push. Those are the tool, not the proposal.

Scanning all 60 backlog titles, the convention set is:

In `## Todo`: **#1** (hard rule 8 to prose style, plus hyphenation), **#2** (the agent-files are the proposal), and the new restart entry.

In the backlog, cited by title per #58's own doctrine:

- **Move the satellites' why into rationale.md.** `jj.md`, `prose.md`, `notes.md`, and `versioning.md` still carry inline "Why:" paragraphs. The largest of the set and pure structure.
- **Promote body shape into hard rule 9?** Deferred at the 2026-08-07 convergence for being two days old. The form was pinned at the commit-body-form rung, so the deferral has expired and only the promotion question is left.
- **What carries a Todo entry** and **Cite a Todo or backlog entry by its bold title, not its number.** The second treats a symptom of the first, so deciding the carrier first avoids writing the citation rule twice.
- **Write down what an interlude is.**
- **Sweep the Todo files for pre-0.80 names and retired conventions.** Not a rule change, but the records should say what the rules say before the payload takes them.
- **Update the template payload, and empty the three-way diff.** This one is the terminus rather than a peer: its acceptance check is the three-way comparison going empty, which is exactly "the proposal was accepted and both members re-synced". Everything above has to land before it can run.

One soft ordering note: the prose-style cycle touches `jj.md` for the hyphenation sites, and **Move the satellites' why into rationale.md** rewrites all four satellites, so running prose-style first keeps the second from re-touching what the first just moved.

Two housekeeping facts that bear on whichever entry opens first: `chores-18.md` has seven unfilled `[[N]]` rungs and `chores-16.md` records the freshen cycle's sixteen as still outstanding, all due at the next opening's step 1, and backlog **`validate`: fail on an unfilled `[[N]]` rung whose commit is on `main`** is the tooling that would stop that accumulating.

8. **Tiered exit status for `config --validate`** (wink, 2026-08-12). Today every failure is
   `ExitCode::FAILURE`: a misspelled key and a config the tool could not read exit alike, so a
   caller can branch on "clean or not" and nothing finer. Proposed: **0** all tables and keys
   known and their values reasonable, **1** unknown or otherwise non-fatal findings, **2** a
   fatal situation. The convention is grep's and diff's, so it needs no teaching.
   - the fatal cases already exist and are the subject of bugs.md's **`config --validate`
     reports "I gave up" as a finding** (#9): malformed TOML, an unclosed fence, a side holding
     both carriers, a legacy `[workspace]` schema. Every one of them means the check could not
     be performed rather than that it failed
   - **sequenced after that bug**, which draws the "found something" / "could not check"
     distinction as a local fix. Once drawn, the exit status is a rendering of it, and doing
     the tiering first would mean inventing the classification twice
   - the cost is not in `config`: `main` maps every subcommand error to `ExitCode::FAILURE`
     (`main.rs:477`, `:507`, `:514`), so a distinct code needs the error path every subcommand
     shares. Cheapest to take while that path is open for another reason
   - tier 0's "values reasonable" describes a capability that does not exist: `key_known`
     compares key paths only and no value is ever inspected. Read tier 0 as "keys known" at
     the start, and value checks land later as ordinary tier-1 findings
   - decide there: whether `--refresh --check`'s difference exit joins this scheme (a
     difference is a finding, not a fatal) or keeps its own
9. **`config --toml`: print the TOML a markdown carrier yields** (iiac-perf + bot,
   2026-08-12). The md carrier costs a config file the toml-aware editors and formatters a
   `.toml` gets, and nothing answers "what do these fences actually concatenate to?", which is
   also the question a parse diagnostic raises. Outside the "docs: freshen vc-config and
   config subcmd" ladder, whose acceptance items do not need it, but ranked here because a
   format's debugger is worth most while the format is new.
   - run the `md_fence` filter over the target file and print the result verbatim, blanks
     included, so the printed line numbers are the source's and a diagnostic's line lands
   - **not `--resolved`**, iiac-perf's word: this subcommand already spends "resolved" on
     effective-after-layering (the `[repos]` resolved-agreement invariant, `resolved_hint`'s
     which-carrier-exists answer), and this is the far end of that, one file's raw extraction
     before any parse or layering
   - it has no existing surface to join: `config` with no flag prints the *schema*, not a
     workspace's values, so nothing today shows a config file's own contents at all
   - decide there: the name (`--toml`, `--as-toml`, `--fences`), and whether it composes with
     `--validate` or excludes it

content.content:
22. **config: extract flag-backed key descriptions from Clap.**
    `config`'s key descriptions live in `config_schema.rs`
    (`doc`/`used_by`). For the handful of keys that map 1:1 to a
    CLI flag (`bot-session.col-width` ↔ `--col-width`,
    `--result-lines`), the description could instead be pulled
    from the Clap arg's help via `Cli::command()` introspection,
    so `vc-x1 config` and `--help` share one source and can't
    disagree.
    - Only ~2 keys map cleanly (most are config-only, flag-sets,
      or value-providers), so it's a partial source and the
      schema stays authoritative for the rest.
    - Defaults still come from the schema/consts (the args
      dropped `default_value_t`, so Clap no longer holds them).
    - Output format is unchanged, only the text source, so no
      rework of the 0.71.0-9 rendering.
23. **Stale `/.vc-x1` gitignore line: report it, and a safer revert, if ever.** The 0.78.3
    residue. Existing workspaces keep their `/.vc-x1` `.gitignore` line: never edit the
    user's file automatically. Report that the line is no longer needed and leave the
    removal to them (which surface runs the check is TBD, and `config --validate` and the
    proposed `validate-repo` are the candidates). Separately, any `revert` reintroduction first
    needs the op-log-derived design: identifiable sync operations, target the parent of the
    run's earliest op, preview and confirm, refuse on intervening non-sync operations.
    Background in
    [chores-16](notes/chores/chores-16.md#refactor-drop-sync-state-and-remove-revert).
24. **Move the agent-files' inline whys to rationale.md.** (wink, 2026-08-23) rationale.md
    holds AGENTS.md's whys and, since the advance-patch-by-default rung, a per-file section
    for versioning.md. The other agent-files (jj.md, notes.md, prose.md, messaging.md) still
    carry inline "Why:" paragraphs, burdening the rule files the split exists to keep concise.
    Sweep them into rationale.md per-file sections, one heading per rule, and leave
    `[why](rationale.md#<slug>)` links behind. Filed at the halve cycle, ranked here so it
    stops living only in a chores narrative.
25. **Semicolon rule: name the whole-file exemption or schedule the sweep.** (wink,
    2026-08-21) prose.md's Semicolons converts a touched file's prose semicolons whole-file,
    but the living records (TODO.md, README.md, the chores files) are touched every cycle and
    never converted, 57 and 64 sites at the 2026-08-21 count. Either the rule names the
    exemption, files every cycle touches are swept rather than converted on touch, or the
    sweep is scheduled. Until then the working rule: a line you write or edit carries none,
    the rest of the file waits. Drained from the dogfood log at its retirement.
26. **`vc-x1 validate --full`: accept the default by name.** (wink, 2026-08-21) `full` is the
    `[validate]` table `vc-x1 validate` runs and `--fast` names the other, so `--full` should be
    accepted too, unnecessary but allowed, so a reader of a command sees which table ran.

content.content:
58. **Cite a Todo or backlog entry by its bold title, not its number** (wink, 2026-08-12).
    Numbers are addresses that change on every insert. Ranking two entries in one session
    renumbered 15 in `TODO.md` and slid a backlog entry from 56 to 55, invalidating references
    written minutes earlier, one of them already drafted into another member's mailbox. Titles
    do not move.
    - the doctrine already exists one level up: hard rule 9 makes a cycle step's title its only
      identifier, carrying no number and unambiguous within its cycle. This is the same rule
      applied to the notes files, which is the argument for it being pinned rather than local
    - a number may still ride along as a convenience ("**title** (#5)"), but the title is what
      the reference *is*, so a stale number beside a live title is a hint gone slightly out of
      date rather than a pointer at the wrong entry
    - long titles make a citation unwieldy, which is an argument for keeping them short and a
      reason to allow citing an unambiguous prefix. Commit titles have a 50-char cap and these
      have none, which is where the friction comes from. Decide there whether to cap them
    - the rule has a precondition the files do not meet: every entry needs a bold title and
      titles must be locally unique. Several backlog entries open in bare prose with no bold
      title at all, so the sweep is real work rather than a wording change
    - **the cost is clickability.** A bold title inside a numbered list item is not a heading,
      so it has no anchor and a citation by title cannot be a link. Numbers were never linkable
      either, so nothing regresses, but the fix (entries become `###` headings, which anchors
      and lets `validate-anchors` reach them) is a much larger change and should be decided
      here rather than assumed by whoever does the sweep
    - mechanical check once validate-anchors lands: every entry carries a bold title, and
      titles are unique within their file
    - the rule belongs in pinned `agent-data/notes.md` beside Notes references and Reference
      numbering, so it is a family proposal; a conventions change gets its own small cycle per
      AGENTS.md's Changing the agent-files. Sequenced after validate-anchors, like
      **vc-config.md per-key worked examples**, so the uniqueness sweep is machine-verified
    - the bold-title precondition is done (2026-08-12): all 56 entries here carry one, none
      duplicated. What remains is the rule, the citation sweep, and the check

59. **What carries a Todo entry: numbered list, heading, or a tracker outside the repo?**
    (wink, 2026-08-12). The numbered-list form is what makes numbers unstable and titles
    unlinkable, so **Cite a Todo or backlog entry by its bold title, not its number** (#56)
    treats a symptom of it. Three routes, and they are not the same size of decision.
    - **`###` headings per entry.** Every entry gains an anchor, so a citation becomes a link,
      `validate-anchors` reaches it, and the bold-title rule enforces itself structurally
      because a heading *is* the title. The cost is the numbering machinery: `fix-todo` and
      validate-numbering key on `^\d+\. `, and `TODO.md`'s own header tells intro paragraphs to
      lead with a space so they miss that pattern. Strict rank becomes document order, which
      loses nothing. The move between files stays a cut-paste
    - **GitHub issues.** A real tracker: state, search, assignment, comments, and cross-repo
      references between members. It would also subsume the mailbox, which exists only because
      a member cannot write into another member's repo
    - **A database.** Everything the issues route costs, plus building and maintaining the tool,
      minus a free tracker. It wins only under a query load that 78 entries do not present
    - **the crux is doctrine, not format.** AGENTS.md keeps durable context in committed files
      because "easy for everyone to find beats convenient for the bot alone". Issues and a db
      both leave the repo: not in the diff, not in jj history, not in a clone, not offline, not
      carried by the template payload, and the one-home-per-record move (a `## In Progress`
      block becoming a chores section at close-out) turns into a sync problem across two
      systems. So headings are a change inside the doctrine and the other two are a change *to*
      it, which is a decision to take deliberately rather than as a file-format tweak
    - a narrower version of the issues route may survive that objection: issues for
      *cross-member coordination*, where the mailbox is already a workaround for repo
      boundaries, and files for in-repo records. Worth separating before the whole idea is
      accepted or rejected
    - **decide this before the citation sweep**, since headings would change what the sweep
      does: with anchors, citations become links and the bold-title rule is restated rather
      than applied as written
    - **a second motivation, from the mailbox rather than the notes files** (wink,
      2026-08-12): handling a message deletes it, which is heavy-handed for anything a commit
      might later want to cite, and the copy-into-records-first rule exists precisely because
      deletion loses the original. A durable, referenceable issue would serve both surfaces at
      once, which strengthens the tracker option relative to headings, since headings fix
      citation inside a repo and do nothing for cross-member traffic

### docs: the family agent-files proposal

Program record. **No cycle is open**: none of the opening's steps have run. When we pick the
first cycle it becomes a `####` under this heading carrying the six items, per
[The In Progress block](agent-data/notes.md#the-in-progress-block).

The pinned agent-files carry local decisions the family has not agreed, and two more surfaced

downstream sees the work and the members cannot re-sync.

Run the convention entries as a series of small docs cycles, each its own cycle per
[Changing the agent-files](AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files), then update the template payload
and re-sync both members.

#### Acceptance check

The three-way comparison between the two members and the payload goes empty, which is the check
the last cycle already names.

One docs cycle per rung, in a proposed order not yet agreed. A rung's `[[N]]` fills with that
cycle's chores section, not with a single commit.

Two decisions, one new rule, and two scope corrections.

One subsection per rung, headed by the rung's exact title.

Hard rule 8 is "Typeable punctuation", the narrowest of a family of prose rules. Widen it to
"Prose style" so it also carries no wall-of-prose (intro plus bullets and sub-bullets instead),
the one-spelling-per-term rule, and the semicolon question below.

##### Restart the session after a close-out

After a close-out wink exits the agent and restarts it, so the next cycle opens on a fresh
context. Not a hard rule, but a requirement in practice: a long context degrades recall, and a
close-out is the one boundary where nothing is in flight, so the restart costs nothing.

import re, io

def split_entries(lines, start, end):
    """Return (preamble, [(num, [lines])]) for the region lines[start:end]."""
    idx = [i for i in range(start, end) if re.match(r'^\d+\.\s', lines[i])]
    pre = lines[start:idx[0]]
    ents = []
    for k, i in enumerate(idx):
        j = idx[k+1] if k+1 < len(idx) else end
        ents.append((int(re.match(r'^(\d+)\.', lines[i]).group(1)), lines[i:j]))
    return pre, ents

def to_subbullet(el):
    w = len(re.match(r'^\d+\.\s+', el[0]).group(0))
    out = ['   - ' + el[0][w:]]
    for ln in el[1:]:
        out.append('     ' + ln[w:] if ln.strip() else ln)
    while out and not out[-1].strip():
        out.pop()
    return out

# ---------------- TODO.md ----------------
lines = open('TODO.md').read().split('\n')
ip = open('tmp/ip.md').read().rstrip('\n').split('\n')

b0 = lines.index('### docs: the family agent-files proposal')
b1 = lines.index('## Todo')
t1 = lines.index('## Ideas')
pre, ents = split_entries(lines, b1, t1)
by = dict(ents)

CONFIG = [4, 3, 9, 5, 8, 22]
MOVED  = [1, 2, 24, 25]
head = ['1. **The vc-config program: finish the surface, then shrink it.** The markdown carrier',
        '   landed and the rest of the config subcommand\'s work was spread across six entries. They',
        '   share one surface, one schema and one set of tests, so they run as one program rather',
        '   than six rankings. Sub-entries keep their bold titles, so a citation by title still',
        '   resolves.']
cfg = head[:]
for n in CONFIG:
    cfg += to_subbullet(by[n]) + ['']
cfg = cfg[:-1]

keep = [e for e in ents if e[0] not in CONFIG and e[0] not in MOVED]
newtodo = cfg + ['']
for _, el in keep:
    while el and not el[-1].strip():
        el.pop()
    newtodo += el + ['']

out = lines[:b0] + ip + [''] + [lines[b1]] + pre[1:] + newtodo + lines[t1:]
txt = '\n'.join(out)

# references repack: rungs take 1..9, survivors shift
anchors = ['prose-style-hard-rule-8-hyphenation-and-the-semicolon-exemption',
           'restart-the-session-after-a-close-out',
           'the-agent-files-are-the-proposal-customd-the-override',
           'promote-body-shape-into-hard-rule-9',
           'what-carries-a-todo-entry-then-cite-it-by-title',
           'move-the-agent-files-inline-whys-to-rationalemd',
           'write-down-what-an-interlude-is',
           'sweep-the-todo-files-for-pre-080-names-and-retired-conventions',
           'update-the-template-payload-and-empty-the-three-way-diff']
for a, b in (('[[5]]', '[[10]]'), ('[[61]]', '[[11]]'), ('[[60]]', '[[12]]')):
    txt = txt.replace(a, b)
refs = '\n'.join('[%d]: #%s' % (i+1, s) for i, s in enumerate(anchors))
refs += '\n[10]: /notes/forks-multi-user.md'
refs += '\n[11]: /notes/chores/chores-18.md#docs-reshape-at-land'
refs += '\n[12]: /notes/chores/chores-17.md#docs-fix-dev-artifacts'
txt = re.sub(r'# References\n\n.*?$', '# References\n\n' + refs + '\n', txt, flags=re.S)
txt = txt.replace('↔', '<->')
open('TODO.md', 'w').write(txt)

# ---------------- todo-backlog.md ----------------
bl = open('notes/todo-backlog.md').read().split('\n')
s = bl.index('## Todo')
e = bl.index('# References')
pre, ents = split_entries(bl, s, e)
DROP = {2, 3, 48, 52, 58, 59, 60}
new = []
for n, el in ents:
    if n in DROP:
        continue
    while el and not el[-1].strip():
        el.pop()
    new += el + ['']
open('notes/todo-backlog.md', 'w').write('\n'.join(bl[:s] + pre + new + bl[e:]))
print('ok')

1. **The vc-config program: finish the surface, then shrink it.** The markdown carrier
   landed and the rest of the config subcommand's work was spread across six entries. They
   share one surface, one schema and one set of tests, so they run as one program rather
   than six rankings. Sub-entries keep their bold titles, so a citation by title still
   resolves.
   - **Finish the vc-config surface (the five rungs deferred at the 0.78.8 early close).** The
     markdown carrier landed and the cycle closed early for the 0816-proposal agent-files work,
     leaving the surface's completion as its own cycle. The deferred acceptance items ride with
     it: agent vocabulary with old spellings rejected (a test shows the fix-it),
     `config --refresh` with `--check` clean on both sides, `validate-anchors` clean over the
     records, and the `.agent-session` repoint end to end.
     - **feat: agent naming in config and CLI** (moved 2026-08-21 into the "docs: empty
       custom-family into the pinned set and config" ladder, ahead of its schema-tables rung,
       so the new tables are born under the new names, and the notes below ride with it):
       `repos.agent` / `[agent-session]` /
       `agent-session` / `--scope=agent`, old spellings rejected rather than aliased, the
       rejection printing its fix-it for both sides (`legacy_vc_config::reject` is the model)
       - rejection, not aliases (wink, 2026-08-12, iiac-perf concurring): an alias is a live
         dual-name path that stays temporary only if someone later deletes it, while a
         rejection is permanent and harmless. `repos.bot` is a topology key, so the fix-it
         turns the flag day into a five-second edit at a moment the member picks
       - values untouched: `repos.agent = ".claude"` until the repoint rung, and the ochid
         label stays `/.claude/` (test-pinned). The pinned-prose sweep stays excluded
         (convention work runs as its own cycle), and `homes` -> `files` waits for the
         Drop-the-global-config entry below, this rung respelling `workspace-bot` alone
     - **chore: regenerate configs in md format**: `vc-config-test.md` becomes the generated
       model `vc-config-model.md` (generated, not maintained: build.rs already knows every
       key, so "contains every key" holds by construction), the work-side `.vc-config.md`
       byte-identical to it (a test renders and compares), both sides regenerated, and the
       `.vc-x1` leftovers retired (`.claude/.vc-x1`, the work `.gitignore` line)
       - ownership model (2026-08-10): fence interiors are the workspace's own, the prose
         between fences is machine-owned rendering, and the durable link edit is
         `reference-base`, an active key surviving refresh
       - the `homes` correction rides here: the three `bot-session` keys drop the agent side,
         which nothing reads
       - the model carries derived `reference-base` https urls, and the info-string rule's
         negative half (only fences tagged exactly `toml` are live) lands in `vc-config.md`
       - init emits `.vc-config.md` from the generated model for new workspaces (found
         2026-08-19: init still writes `.vc-config.toml`, starting every new member on the
         legacy carrier)
     - **feat: add config --refresh**: regenerate a file's prose while preserving fence

Reviewed `TODO.md:10-69`. The intent is good and two of the changes are genuine corrections. Three things break, one conflicts with the pinned files, and the rest is polish.

## Breaks

- **"Shape:" now dangles.** `TODO.md:68` still ends the `## In Progress` paragraph with "Shape:" and the shape no longer follows it. Either move the Model block back under that paragraph, or change "Shape:" to point up at it.
- **The multi-cycle program paragraph is gone.** It said the program is the `###`, its current cycle the `####`, and the six items one level below. That is the only thing that authorizes the block now sitting in the section. Removing it leaves my program block undocumented. Deliberate, or lost in the edit?
- **The "Full rules in [Opening]... [Chores sections]..." line moved inside the fence**, so both links are now literal text rather than links.

## Conflicts with the pinned files

- **`Cycle details` vs `Ladder details`.** `AGENTS.md` (per-rung flow step 4, Opening step 3) and `notes.md` (the area itself, and the close-out move) all say `Ladder details`. I used `Cycle details` in the program block because a program's rungs really are cycles, and it looks like that name got picked up into the generic model. My suggestion: keep `Ladder details` as the general name, since an ordinary rung is a commit, and let a program block use `Cycle details` as its own variant. If you want the rename family-wide it has to land in `notes.md` and `AGENTS.md` too, which makes it a rung of the proposal rather than a TODO.md edit.
- **The rung subsection's content shape.** The model gives every rung a problem plus solutions. `notes.md` gives a rung's subsection an intent statement at laddering and the conceptual delta at landing, "never a restatement of the landed commit body", and reserves problem/solution form for the *closing* rung's gotchas. Widening it to every rung is a reasonable proposal, but it changes `notes.md`.
  - if it is meant to be commit-body form, the markers are wrong: `prose.md` uses `*` for a problem and `-` for a solution, and the model has the problem as a plain line.
- **The closing subsection has no stub.** `notes.md` says it opens with "Closing out the cycle."

## Notation

- `{...}+`, `{...}0+`, `{...}1+` arrives with no legend, and `+` and `1+` mean the same thing. Pick one spelling and say what it means.
- `<...>` is doing two jobs, placeholder (`<type>: <title>`) and commentary (`<Single-step ladder:>`, `<The (done/current) are added...>`). A reader cannot tell which is which. I would reserve `<...>` for placeholders and write the commentary as plain lines.
- Same inconsistency in the headings: `<##### title>` bracketed in the single-step case, `##### cycle title opening` bare in the multi-step case.

## Small

- `[<title work rung 2][M]` is missing its closing `>`.
- "Solultion" twice.
- "changes it's state" wants "its", and "each ladder" probably wants "each rung".
- The `(done)`/`(current)` note sits under Acceptance check but describes the Ladder, so it reads as belonging to the wrong item.

## Right

- Linking the closing rung, `[<cycle title> closing][M]`, matches `notes.md`. The old model left it unlinked, so this fixes a real disagreement.
- Dropping "five" from Deliberation removes a count that goes stale whenever the item list moves.
- Separating the single-step and multi-step shapes is genuinely useful, and none of the pinned files shows it. Worth carrying into `notes.md` as part of the proposal.

No banned punctuation or semicolons in the block. Nothing edited.

content.text:
You read that more broadly than I meant it, and one of my recommendations was wrong because of it.

Your model is right and it is what `AGENTS.md` Terminology says: a cycle is one change run from opening to closing, "as one commit or a ladder of them". So cycle == rung only in the single-step case. In a multi-step cycle the cycle is the whole set, opening through closing.

What I meant applies at a different level. There are two ladders in play, and a rung means something different on each:

- **A cycle's ladder:** rungs are commits. Single-step is the one-rung case, cycle == rung == commit.
- **A program's ladder:** rungs are cycles. Each rung is a whole cycle, itself single- or multi-step.

The block now in `## In Progress` is the second kind, which is why I wrote `Cycle details` there. I was not claiming cycle == rung in general.

**Where that changes my advice:** "ladder" is the list at either level, and "rung" does not promise what an element is, so `Ladder details` is correct at both. Keeping two names buys nothing and costs a reader a lookup. So the fix is one name everywhere, `Ladder details`, and my program block should be renamed to match rather than the model bending toward mine. That drops the conflict I flagged entirely, with no change to `notes.md` or `AGENTS.md`.

One other correction from that review: I said the deleted multi-cycle program paragraph was the only thing authorizing the current block. It is not. `notes.md`'s "The In Progress block" carries that rule, and TODO.md's copy was a paraphrase of it, so dropping it is fine and arguably better under one-home-per-text.

The rest of the review stands: the dangling "Shape:", the links now buried in the fence, the rung subsection's content shape against `notes.md`, the missing closing stub, the `{...}+` legend, `<...>` doing two jobs, and the small typos.

content.text:
Thoughts only, nothing edited. Read it as a first-time agent would.

## The syntax problem: `<...>` does four jobs

That's the one that actually blocks a reader. Right now `<...>` means:

- substitute this: `<type>: <title>`, `<what is wrong, a sentence or two>`
- read this, don't write it: `<The (done/current) are added...>`, `<Full rules in [Opening]...>`
- pick one of these two shapes: `<Single-step ladder:>`, `<Multi-step ladder:>`
- and a heading that is itself a placeholder: `<##### title>`

An agent can't tell "replace" from "read". Give each job its own marker: `<...>` for substitution only, and a `#` comment line for everything else, which reads as a comment in almost every language.

The same inconsistency shows inside one section: `<##### title>` is bracketed in the single-step case and `##### cycle title opening` is bare in the multi-step case, and both are headings you write.

## `{...}1+` is undefined, and probably unnecessary

No legend, and `1+` appears twice against one `0+`. Then `{...}1+ Repeat as needed` glosses the notation in words right after using it, which is the tell that the notation isn't earning its keep. Either add a two-line legend at the top of the fence, or drop the braces and say it in a `#` comment. I'd drop them.

The braces also don't survive plain text. In the multi-step case the `{` opens on the same line as `#####` and the `}1+` closes after an indented bullet two lines later. A reader could reasonably copy `{##### title work rung 1` into their file.

## The two shapes are really one rule

This is the biggest simplification available. Everything above `Ladder details` is identical between single-step and multi-step, and the rule under it is just **one subsection per rung**. A single-step cycle has one rung, so it gets one subsection. Nothing else differs.

So the single/multi split belongs in the **Ladder**, not in `Ladder details`, and it is two comment lines there. That deletes about half the `Ladder details` block and removes both mode selectors.

## The rung body still disagrees with notes.md

Flagged before and unchanged: the model gives every rung a problem plus a `-` solution, while `notes.md` gives a rung's subsection an intent statement at laddering and the conceptual delta at landing, reserving problem/solution form for the closing rung's gotchas. One of them has to move. If the model wins, that is a rung of this proposal, not a TODO.md edit.

If you do mean commit-body form there, the markers are wrong: `prose.md` uses `*` for a problem and `-` for a solution, and the model's problem line carries no marker.

## A sketch, since showing beats describing

```
In Progress model. <X> substitute. # comment, not content.

## In Progress

### <type>: <cycle title>

#### Problem
<what is wrong, a sentence or two>

#### Solution
<what will be done about it, broad, provisional until the close-out>

#### Acceptance check
<the measure of "are you finished?">

#### Ladder
# multi-step: bookends, plus one rung per commit between them
# single-step: one rung carrying the bare cycle title, no bookends
# (current) is set at the rung's first edit, flipped to (done) at its describe
- [[N]] [<cycle title> opening][1] (done)
- [[N]] [<work rung title>][2] (current)
- [[N]] [<work rung title>][3]
- [[N]] [<cycle title> closing][4]

#### Deliberation
<how the above were decided, or `_None._` if there was nothing to deliberate>

#### Ladder details
# one subsection per rung, in ladder order, headed by the rung's exact title

##### <rung title>
<the rung's intent at laddering, its conceptual delta at landing>

##### <cycle title> closing
Closing out the cycle.
```

Two changes worth noting in it. `[M]` became `[1]`-`[4]`, since one repeated `M` reads as a single shared slot when each rung actually gets its own. And the closing subsection shows `notes.md`'s stub, which the current model omits.

## The example link: yes, and make it the main teaching device

Agreed, and I'd rank it above the model for the acquaint case. A model teaches the skeleton. Everything a first-time agent still can't get from it comes from a real one: what belongs in a rung subsection, that `[[N]]` stays literal until backfill, that the rung title is verbatim-identical to the commit title and the chores header.

Two links, both **below** the fence so they render:

- Worked example: `notes/chores/chores-18.md#docs-reshape-at-land`, the most recent close-out. Say that a chores section is the block *after* the close-out move, so its headings sit one level up and its refs are renumbered.
- Rules: `AGENTS.md#opening` and `agent-data/notes.md#the-in-progress-block`.

The `<Full rules in [Opening]...>` footer is currently inside the fence, so both links are dead text. That's the same fix.

## Two structural questions

- **Make it a heading.** "In Progress model:" is better than "Model:", but as a bare line it has no anchor. `## In Progress model` costs nothing and lets `AGENTS.md` and `notes.md` link to it by name.
- **Should it live in TODO.md at all?** A skeleton of the In Progress block is a rule, and pinned files hold rules while project records hold records. Today `notes.md` describes the block in prose with no skeleton, and TODO.md has the skeleton but isn't pinned, so no other family member gets it. Moving the model into `agent-data/notes.md` and leaving a link here would give it one home and carry it to the family. That feels like it belongs to the **What carries a Todo entry** rung, or its own.

## Small

- `[<title work rung 2][M]` is missing its closing `>`.
- "Solultion" twice.
- "changes it's state" wants "its", and "each ladder" probably wants "each rung".
- The `(done)`/`(current)` note sits above `#### Ladder`, so it reads as a body line for Acceptance check.

Read the `@--` body and compared it against the same rung's subsection in `chores-18.md:180`. Your instinct is right, and the gap is bigger than a formatting difference.

## They are not similar today

Same rung, two records:

**Commit body:** intro stating the problem, then three `*` facets, each with its `-` solutions. Every bullet's role is readable from its marker.

**Chores subsection:** intro stating *what was built* rather than a problem, then a flat `-` list of five. Three are content facts, the fourth packs structure, range mode and delegation into one long bullet, the fifth is a placement decision. Nothing says which bullet answers what.

The body is the better-organized of the two. That is the argument for making the subsection follow it rather than the reverse.

## The shape to share, and the difference to keep

Same skeleton, different altitude:

- **Rung subsection:** intro, `*` facets, `-` solutions, and it may carry a **third level** under a `-` for the design point, alternative, consequence or deferral.
- **Commit body:** the same skeleton compressed. No third level, no deliberation, which `prose.md` already bans from a body.

That makes "succinct, not verbatim" concrete and checkable: **the body is the subsection with the third level dropped and the prose tightened.** It also keeps `notes.md`'s division intact, because the third level is exactly the design thinking chores is supposed to own.

## The part that makes it worth doing

The shape carries the timing:

- **At laddering** you know the problem, so you write the intro and the `*` facets.
- **At landing** you know what you did, so you fill the `-` solutions.
- **At describe**, per-rung flow step 7, you compress to the body.

That is a fill, not a rewrite. Today `notes.md` asks for an "intent statement" at laddering and a "conceptual delta" at landing, which are two different texts, so the agent writes the subsection twice and then invents a third shape for the commit. Sharing the skeleton collapses three authoring moments into one form filled in two passes.

## What it costs in the pinned files

- `notes.md`, "The In Progress block": the `Ladder details` paragraph. Its "never a restatement of the landed commit body" inverts to "the body is this, compressed". A real edit, and a rung of this cycle.
- `prose.md`, Commit-body form: one sentence saying the form is shared with the rung subsection and the body is the compression.
- `notes.md`, "Chores section content" survives unchanged. Its division still holds.
- Existing subsections convert when touched, no sweep. The gitk one would need a facet above its first three bullets, something like `* Nothing said what each view answers.`

## What `Ladder details` should show

This replaces both the single-step and multi-step blocks, since one rule covers them:

```
#### Ladder details
# one subsection per rung, in ladder order, headed by the rung's exact title
# same shape as the commit body: intro, * facets, - solutions
# at laddering write the intro and the * facets, at landing fill the - solutions
# the commit body is this, compressed: drop the third level and any deliberation

##### <rung title>

<this rung's problem, a sentence or two>

* <a facet of that problem>
  - <what this rung did about it>
  - <another solution to the same facet>
* <another facet>
  - <what this rung did about it>
    - <the design point, alternative or deferral the commit body drops>
```

## On the example link

It resolves, so the mechanics are fine. Two suggestions:

- **Point at the cycle, not the ToC.** `#docs-reshape-at-land` saves a hop, and chores-18 holds one cycle so far, so "some examples" is currently one.
- **Warn about the level shift, or the reader copies it wrong.** A chores section is the block *after* the close-out move, so its headings sit one level up: rungs are `####` there and `#####` in a live block. An agent learning the shape from `chores-18.md` and copying it into `## In Progress` will produce the wrong levels. Worth one clause.

Worth noting there is already a live example needing no translation, the block below it in this same file. A reader wanting "what does a real one look like right now" is better served by that, and `chores-18.md` is better as "what does a finished one look like".

content.text:
Agreed on all three. Two of them sharpen what I said rather than contradict it.

## Single-step and multi-step: real, but not where I put it

We were talking about different sections. The difference is real and it lives in **two** places, neither of them `Ladder details`:

- **The Ladder.** Multi-step has bookends. Single-step is one rung carrying the bare cycle title, which `prose.md` already states: "A single-step cycle's one commit is the cycle and keeps the bare title."
- **The close-out shape.** You're right that a single-step cycle isn't trapezoidal. With one commit all three shapes degenerate: squash has nothing to squash, keep-separate is the one commit, and a trapezoid would build a merge whose second parent is that lone commit, which adds a commit and buys no reachability. So the accurate statement is that **the shape choice does not arise**, and the commit fast-forwards onto `main`.

What I wanted to collapse was only the duplicated block under `Ladder details`, which prints the same rule twice. One subsection per rung covers both, because single-step has one rung. Shown where it belongs:

```
#### Ladder
# multi-step: bookends, one rung per commit between, close-out shape chosen at the close-out
- [[N]] [<cycle title> opening][1] (done)
- [[N]] [<work rung title>][2] (current)
- [[N]] [<cycle title> closing][3]

# single-step: one rung, the bare cycle title, no bookends, no shape choice
- [[N]] [<cycle title>][1]
```

**A gap this surfaces.** `AGENTS.md` Close-out step 5 says to record the shape choice "in the closing rung's subsection". A single-step cycle has no closing rung, so that instruction has nowhere to land. Small, but it is exactly the kind of thing a first-time agent stalls on. Worth a rung of this cycle.

## problem-facet and solution-facet

Better than what I wrote, and better than what `prose.md` has now. Today it says "`*` bullets are the problem's facets" and then just "`-` bullets are solutions", so the naming is asymmetric while the structure is not.

Your reading holds up against the real body. Under one problem-facet:

```
* The gitk reading had no home of its own, so nothing could link to it.
  - jj.md gains Read a change in gitk at full context, with its own anchor: ...
  - README.md's jj Tips for Git Users points at the section, ...
```

Neither `-` is the whole answer. Together they are. So each is a facet of the solution to that problem-facet, and the term is accurate rather than merely symmetric. Both hyphenate under your one-spelling rule, and both grep.

One asymmetry to decide rather than inherit: the problem side has an intro plus its facets, while the solution side has facets and no intro. That is fine in practice, since the problem-facet above already frames them, but the vocabulary should say so plainly instead of implying a missing solution statement. Something like: the intro states the problem, `*` decomposes it into problem-facets, and each problem-facet's answer decomposes into solution-facets.

This is a `prose.md` edit in three spots: the two bullet definitions, and "One facet is the trivial commit", which becomes one problem-facet.

## "what this rung did about it" is too vague

You're right, and the real bodies show what the placeholder should teach. Every solution-facet in that commit follows one pattern: **name the thing that changed, say what it now does, end with what that buys.**

- "jj.md **gains** Read a change in gitk at full context, with its own anchor: ..."
- "README.md's jj Tips for Git Users **points at** the section, **so** the reading is reachable outside any cycle."
- "Preview before choosing **points at** the section instead of repeating it, **leaving** the gitk facts one home."

So the placeholder wants to carry three things, not one. Candidates:

- `<what changed, and what that buys>` — shortest, keeps the two halves.
- `<the file or section, what it now does, and what that buys>` — names the subject explicitly, which is the part the current wording loses.
- `<one part of the answer: what changed, stated as a sentence>` — leans on `prose.md`'s existing rule that these are sentences, not fragments.

I'd take the second. "Named subject" is the discipline that keeps a solution-facet from sliding into a vague claim, and it is the thing every real example does and my placeholder didn't.

content.text:
Direct answer, since you asked me as the consumer: **one thing, with the single-step case named as a short delta, and words rather than notation.**

## Why one thing

Three reasons, the third being the one that decides it for me.

- The pinned file already unifies them. `AGENTS.md` Terminology: a cycle is "one change, run from opening to closing **as one commit or a ladder of them**." Two models in TODO.md would contradict a definition that is already singular.
- Everything but two lines is identical. Problem, Solution, Acceptance check, Deliberation, Ladder details, the per-rung flow, the review stops. Showing two skeletons duplicates ~90% of the text, and duplicated detail drifts. That is the same argument `notes.md` uses to keep one ladder instead of a working one and an as-built one.
- **The boundary is soft and gets crossed mid-cycle.** `AGENTS.md` says a single-step cycle "grows a ladder at no cost". If the model presents two shapes, growing looks like switching models. If it presents one shape with an optional bookend, growing is just adding rungs. Two models would make a soft boundary look hard, which is worse than the duplication.

## Why words

You asked which is easier for me. Words, clearly:

- I read English natively. A custom notation is a second language I have to learn from a legend and then hold in working memory while parsing the skeleton.
- It is used four times. A DSL earns its keep across fifty productions, not four.
- Every notation character you'd pick is also possible literal content. `{`, `}`, `+`, `<`, `>` all appear in real markdown. Notation creates an ambiguity words don't have.
- The failure modes are asymmetric. Misread a word and I write slightly wrong prose. Misread `{Additional info needed}0+` as literal and I write it into the file.

Keep exactly one notation, `<X>` for substitute. It is the most conventional marker in existence, every man page uses it, and it needs no legend.

## The one thing I'd add that isn't in either option

**Make the model's job shape only.** Right now it is also trying to carry timing and content rules, and that is what grew the notation. Split the labor three ways:

- **Model:** the shape. What headings, what order, what markers.
- **Worked example:** density and voice. What a real rung subsection actually sounds like.
- **Pinned rules:** timing and content. When `(current)` flips, what a body may not contain.

The model gets smaller, and the two things it was doing badly get done by things that already exist.

## What I'd want to read

```
## In Progress model

The skeleton of a cycle's block. <X> means substitute. A // line is a note, not content.

## In Progress

### <type>: <cycle title>

#### Problem
<what is wrong, a sentence or two>

#### Solution
<what will be done about it, broad, provisional until the close-out>

#### Acceptance check
<the measure of "are you finished?">

#### Ladder
// One rung per commit, in order.
// Single-step: drop both bookends. The one rung carries the bare cycle title,
// and no close-out shape is chosen, since one commit has nothing to reshape.
- [[N]] [<cycle title> opening][1] (done)
- [[N]] [<work rung title>][2] (current)
- [[N]] [<work rung title>][3]
- [[N]] [<cycle title> closing][4]

#### Deliberation
<how the above were decided, or `_None._` if there was nothing to deliberate>

#### Ladder details
// One subsection per rung, in ladder order, headed by the rung's exact title.
// Same shape as the commit body: the intro states this rung's problem, * bullets
// are its problem-facets, - bullets under each are that facet's solution-facets.

##### <rung title>

<this rung's problem, a sentence or two>

* <one problem-facet>
  - <the file or section, what it now does, and what that buys>
  - <another solution-facet of the same problem-facet>
* <another problem-facet>
  - <the file or section, what it now does, and what that buys>
    - <the design point or deferral the commit body drops>
```

Then below the fence, where links actually render:

- a finished example, `chores-18.md#docs-reshape-at-land`, noting its headings sit one level up
- the live example, the block right below
- the rules, `AGENTS.md#opening` and `agent-data/notes.md#the-in-progress-block`

## The one choice I'd hand back to you

The comment marker. I used `//` because `#` is markdown's own heading character and this skeleton is full of `#` lines, so a `#` note sitting next to `#### Ladder` reads as a heading at a glance. `//` has no such collision and reads as a comment everywhere. If `//` feels foreign in a markdown file, the alternative is to move the notes out of the fence entirely and key them by heading name below it. That is more markdown-native and keeps the skeleton pure, at the cost of making me look in two places instead of one. I prefer locality, so `//` inline, but it is a taste call and either works.

content.text:
Good question, and the two markers are not symmetric, so the answer isn't "pick either".

## `<...>` can't be dropped

It is the only one that works **mid-line**, where literal characters and substituted text share a line. The three lines that matter most in the skeleton are all that shape:

```
### <type>: <cycle title>
- [[N]] [<work rung title>][2] (current)
##### <rung title>
```

Those are exactly the lines where the literal characters are fiddly and worth getting right: `[[N]]`, the `][2]` slot, `(current)`, the heading depth. A `//` note is line-oriented, so it can say "the heading is the type, a colon, and the cycle title" but it cannot show you the line. You'd end up writing the note *and* an example, which is more text than the placeholder was.

## `//` can be dropped, but only by relocating the notes

If notes stay in the fence and wear `<...>`, you are back to the overload I flagged first: a bracketed line sometimes means "write here" and sometimes means "read this", and nothing distinguishes them. `<The (done/current) are added as each ladder changes its state>` is exactly that ambiguity in the current model.

So the real fork is:

- **One marker:** `<...>` only, notes move **below** the fence as prose keyed by heading name. Clean skeleton, working links, two places to look.
- **Two markers:** `<...>` inline for substitution, `//` for notes, everything in one place. Each marker has one job, so no ambiguity, but you learn two.

Both are honest. What is not available is one marker with the notes still inside.

## A measurement that decides it

I checked the line budget. The model is `TODO.md:10-59`, fifty lines. `notes.md` makes the routine acquaint read `TODO.md` at `offset=0, limit=60`. So today the model consumes fifty of those sixty lines and **`## In Progress` at line 61 falls outside the acquaint read entirely.** The routine read now shows the model and none of the actual cycle.

That reframes the question. Adding notes below the fence makes it worse, and inline `//` notes make it worse too. Both options are fighting over a budget the model should not be spending.

## So, something else

Move the model into `agent-data/notes.md`, beside "The In Progress block", and leave a one-line link in `TODO.md`. Then:

- The marker question dissolves. There is no sixty-line budget in `notes.md`, so notes can be adjacent **and** the fence stays clean. I would take `//` inline there, for locality.
- `TODO.md`'s acquaint read goes back to being the live cycle and the top of the ranked list, which is what it is for.
- The model reaches the family. It is a rule about the block's shape, and pinned files carry rules while project records carry records. Right now every member has `notes.md`'s prose description and only this repo has the skeleton.
- `notes.md` currently describes the block in words with no skeleton, and the skeleton is the half that words do badly. They belong in one place.

That is a rung of the cycle already in flight rather than a TODO.md edit, which is the right size for it.

content.text:
Yes, and I think it's better than a marked-up skeleton. Honest assessment of why.

## Why a real example beats a skeleton, for me

- **Pattern-matching is what I'm best at.** "Here is one instance, produce another" is a far more reliable instruction to me than "here is a grammar, instantiate it."
- **It shows density and voice**, which a skeleton structurally cannot. `<a sentence or two>` tells me a length. An actual Problem paragraph tells me the register, how much context to assume, whether to name files.
- **It removes the worst failure mode of both markers**, which is writing the placeholder into the file. There is nothing to accidentally copy that isn't already valid.

## The one thing an example can't disambiguate

`[[N]]`. In a filled example, every other token is obviously either literal (`####`, `- `) or content (titles, prose). `[[N]]` is the only one that looks like content but is literally the two characters `[[N]]`, kept until backfill. That is the single most confusing token in the format.

`notes.md` already states it in prose: "the literal `[[N]]` is the as-built ladder's placeholder, filled only at backfill after landing". So it's covered, but it is the sentence that has to survive any rewrite.

Everything else the prose already handles by naming parts and quoting tokens in backticks, which answers your second question: **no, the description needs no meta characters either.** It says "the Ladder", "the Problem", and quotes `(current)` and `[[N]]`. That is exactly how `notes.md`'s existing prose is already written.

## What the example can't show, so prose must

One example is one shape. The single-step case has no bookends and its one rung carries the bare cycle title, so that's a sentence in the prose, not a second example. Same for the close-out-shape point you made.

## Fabricated, not linked, and that's forced

## In Progress

### refactor: extract config loader

#### Problem

Config parsing lives inside the CLI entry point, so every subcommand that wants a setting
reaches through `main` for it, and a test cannot load a config without building the CLI.

#### Solution

Move config loading into its own module with a single `load` entry point that the CLI and the
tests call alike.

#### Acceptance check

`cargo test` passes with a new test that loads a config from a fixture file without touching
`main`, and `vc-x1 config --validate` reports the same findings as before the move.

#### Ladder

- [[N]] [refactor: extract config loader opening][1] (done)
- [[N]] [refactor: split loader from parser][2] (current)
- [[N]] [refactor: extract config loader closing][3]

#### Deliberation

- one work rung, not two: the parser and the loader were going to be split first and moved
  second, but the move is what forces the split, so doing them together is fewer edits
- the acceptance check compares `config --validate` output rather than asserting on internals,
  so a later rename inside the module does not invalidate it

#### Ladder details

##### refactor: extract config loader opening

The cycle's setup commit: backfill the previous cycle's rungs, create and publish the
bookmark, move the Todo entry into this block, and bump the version-of-record.

##### refactor: split loader from parser

Loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load without parsing and a test
cannot parse without a file on disk.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config/loader.rs` finds and reads the file, returning the text and its path, so a
    caller that only wants to know which file was read stops here.
  - `config/parser.rs` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands it a string and
    never touches the filesystem.
    - the error type stays shared for now, since splitting it would change the messages
      `config --validate` prints and the acceptance check compares them
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field access moves behind
    the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows the file's shape.

##### refactor: extract config loader closing

Closing out the cycle.

# References

[1]: #refactor-extract-config-loader-opening
[2]: #refactor-split-loader-from-parser
[3]: #refactor-extract-config-loader-closing
EOF

content.text:
Moved. `agent-data/cycle-model-1.md`, with `TODO-1.md`'s link repointed and the model's own links now relative to its new directory. Working copy only.

On the worry: your feeling is accurate, and the reacquaint at the top of this session is the evidence. I read `AGENTS.md`, `custom.md`, and six of the seven `agent-data` files because the File map lists them and hard rule 0 chains them. I did **not** read `rationale.md`, because the map says it is "never needed to apply" a rule. And I did not follow a single one of the hundred-odd inline `[why](...)`, `[The per-rung flow](...)` style links during that read. I followed links only when a task later pointed at one.

So the honest model of my behavior is:

- **A file named in a read list gets read.** The File map worked exactly as designed.
- **An inline link does not get followed on a first pass.** It registers as "detail exists there", and I come back only when the work needs it.
- **A link at the moment of action does get followed**, because hard rule 7 says to read the step from the file before acting, and that instruction has a trigger.

That gives a clean answer to the three-file question. The spread is fine **if and only if the model file is on the read list.** If it exists only as a link from `notes.md` and `TODO.md`, my own behavior says it will not be read at acquaint, and the first-time agent will build a block from `notes.md`'s prose and get the shape half wrong.

So two edits, not a merge:

- **Add it to the File map in `AGENTS.md`**, with a cue like the others: "the In Progress block, shown. Before opening a cycle." Then it is read the way the other seven are.
- **Name it at the moment of action**: Opening step 3 says "shape it as that section says" and points at `notes.md`. Point that at the model instead, because step 3 is exactly when a link gets followed.

And yes, I think this generalizes to a real weakness in `AGENTS.md`. Its links come in two kinds that look identical: `[why](...)` links, which are correctly optional, and links that carry the *operative* rule, like `[Commit-body form]` at describe step 7 or `[Land]` at close-out step 6. Nothing marks which is which, so both get the same treatment, which is "later, maybe". Hard rule 7 patches this for two of them by name. The general fix is for a step that depends on linked text to say so in the step: "read X first" rather than "see X". A cue with a trigger is what gets followed.

The three-file spread is the right shape, since the model is a rule and belongs pinned. It just needs to be *listed*, not merely *linked*.

Honest walk-through of both cases, because they end in the same place.

**"Read Todo #1."** I read `TODO.md`. That tells me *what* the entry asks for. It tells me nothing about cycles: the In Progress section says "a cycle's record has one home" and shows the shape, but the *rule* that a Todo entry becomes a cycle, that a cycle opens with a bookmark and a version bump, and that a rung goes through a work review and a description review, is not in `TODO.md` at all.

**"Let's solve problem blah."** I don't even open `TODO.md` for the rule. I'd grep it for a matching entry, but the notion of In Progress and ladders doesn't come from there.

In both cases it comes from **`AGENTS.md`**, the one file every session reads before anything. Its Cycle protocol says every change is a cycle, and Opening step 3 says "move every line of the chosen `## Todo` entry into the In Progress block and shape it as that section says", pointing at `notes.md`. That is the only place the notion is born, and it holds regardless of how you phrase the request.

So `TODO-1.md`'s link is not what teaches me. It is documentation for a human reading `TODO.md` cold, and for an agent it is a courtesy pointer at best. Fine to keep, not load-bearing.

Which reduces the "three files" worry to one file. The model must be named in `AGENTS.md`, twice, for the two reasons that came out earlier:

- **File map**, so it is read at acquaint like the other pinned files.
- **Opening step 3**, so it is re-read at the moment of action, which is the hard-rule-7 pattern and the link I will actually follow.

`notes.md` links to it too, but as a peer, not as the entry point.

One gap the "solve problem blah" case exposes, worth a line in the Opening: step 3 assumes a `## Todo` entry exists. When the request arrives in conversation there is none. `messaging.md` already has the rule for the mailbox case, "a request becomes an entry before anything is done about it", and it should apply to a spoken request the same way: write the entry, then open. Otherwise the block gets built with nothing to move into it, and the record has no origin.

Agreed, and that is cleaner than what I proposed. A Todo entry written only to be moved seconds later is a copy, and the block is the one home anyway.

And yes, `AGENTS.md` needs to say both, because today it says only one. Opening step 3 reads "move every line of the chosen `## Todo` entry into the In Progress block", so a spoken request has no path. An agent following it literally either invents a Todo entry to satisfy the wording, which is what I did above, or skips the step because nothing matches.

The fix is one step with two sources, both ending in `TODO.md`:

> 3. In Progress block: write the cycle's record into `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, shaped per the model. A picked-up `## Todo` entry moves there whole, never copied. A request made in conversation is written there directly, and the six items are drafted from what was said.

Two things that wording gets right that a two-case list would not:

- **The block is the destination in both cases.** The reader learns the invariant, one record in one home, and the source is the only variable.
- **The conversation case gets an authoring cue.** "Drafted from what was said" is the reminder that the Problem and Acceptance check are the agent's to write and the user's to review, which is exactly where a spoken request is most likely to be under-recorded.

`notes.md`'s In Progress section has the same one-source wording, "the picked-up `## Todo` item is moved here", and gets the same line.

One thing not to lose: the conversation case still leaves its origin unrecorded once the block moves to chores. A Todo entry carried a date and sometimes a "(wink, ...)" attribution.
